Some temperature movement is normal because the grill cooks to an average temperature, and on a typical good weather day it should generally stay within ±25°F. Larger swings can occur at lower temperatures and with Super Smoke. If you’re seeing swings beyond that, fresh pellets are a great place to start. Pellets should have a slight sheen and snap when broken, and the hopper should be free of excess sawdust. Also check that airflow is not restricted, keep at least 1 inch of clearance around pans or food, make sure any foil is tightly fitted to the drip tray, and avoid opening the lid frequently or changing the temperature repeatedly. Proper startup and shutdown are also important, as is keeping the grill clean. Finally, inspect the drip tray and heat baffle for severe warping, holes, or incorrect placement, and check that the temperature sensor is not bent, damaged, or touching another part of the grill. Bought the Pro Series 34 yesterday and seasoned per the instructions. Started it up early this morning and began smoking a Boston butt at 4am, at 250°F.  Everything was fine for several hours, until the igniter stopped working. Unfortunately I didn't notice it right away, and temperature in the cooking chamber dropped to 143°F before in realized what happened. This of course was frustrating, but I removed everything from inside the grill, cleared the fire pot of pellets and restarted the grill. After 12 hours of cook time at 250°F, the meat probe was barely reaching 170°F. I've never had a butt take that long to cook. I checked it with my own thermometer and found it was actually 20° lower than the Traeger probe was indicating.  I then laid that probe on the cooking grate and closed the lid. The cooking chamber temperature as indicated on the meat probe was 20° lower than the temperature shown on the probe used for the controller. That's a total of 40° difference. I had to move the meat into my oven to finish it off.  I am now 14 hours in and just crossed over 180° as I type this.  My 4th of July celebration has been completely ruined thanks to this. This grill was the biggest waste of money, and that's saying something because I've given money to that Nigerian prince before.  

I will be returning this grill to Home Depot tomorrow and buying something else, from a different company.

ClientResponses.Response: Hello, and thanks for your feedback on the Pro 22. Anytime a pellet grill cannot hold heat, it is almost always going to be for a specific, fixable reason. And while making sure that there are enough pellets in the hopper is important, this is really not one of the more common causes since it is typically the first thing checked. More likely, it is occurring either because there is a substantial accumulation of wood dust at the bottom of the hopper, the pellets have become compromised by moisture, the chimney cap is set too low, or in very rare cases, a specific component is not working correctly, but this will usually prevent the grill from igniting at all. To verify if it is pellets or dust, try clearing out the hopper (through the evacuation door on the back) and make sure that there isn't a lot of fine wood dust blocking the opening to the auger at the bottom. If not, refill the hopper with fresh pellets and try the grill again, but make sure that the chimney cap has a ¾” gap between the bottom rim and the top edge of the smokestack. Once you have the grill started, make note of the initial reading on the controller to confirm that it is within 20 degrees of the ambient air temperature. You should also hear the sound of the induction fan spinning under the bottom of the hopper, which is required for proper airflow to the fire. But if all of this seems to be good, or you would just rather have someone help with the process, please reach out to Traeger Customer Service at 1-800-TRAEGER, any day of the year up until 10:00 PM MT.
